content.narrative_summary: Chronic coronary disease (CCD) encompasses both obstructive and nonobstructive coronary artery disease (CAD), with or without prior myocardial infarction (MI) or revascularization, ischemic heart disease diagnosed noninvasively, and chronic angina syndromes. In the United States, approximately 20.1 million persons live with CCD; 11.1 million have chronic stable angina, and about one-quarter of all MIs occur in the 8.8 million individuals with CCD and a prior MI. Despite a ~25% decline in coronary heart disease mortality over the past decade, CCD remains the leading cause of death globally and imposes substantial individual, economic, and societal burdens. The prevalence of CCD and stable angina varies by age, sex, race, ethnicity, geographic region, and is influenced by social determinants of health. Since the 2012 ACCF/AHA/ACP/AATS/PCNA/SCAI/STS guideline, healthcare expenditures for CCD remain high, and the number and complexity of comorbid conditions (e.g., chronic kidney disease coexisting with CCD) have increased. The intersection of CCD with atrial fibrillation has informed antiplatelet and anticoagulation strategies. With population aging and improving CCD and cancer survival, the field of cardio-oncology has emerged to address these intersecting chronic conditions.

rows.recommendation: In patients with CCD and a change in symptoms or functional capacity that persists despite GDMT, stress positron emission tomography/single photon emission CT myocardial perfusion imaging (PET/SPECT MPI), cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging, or stress echocardiography is recommended to detect the presence and extent of myocardial ischemia, estimate risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and guide therapeutic decision-making.*1–23

In patients with CCD and a change in symptoms or functional capacity that persists despite GDMT, invasive coronary angiography (ICA) is recommended for guiding therapeutic decision-making with the goal of improving anginal symptoms.*24–28

In patients with CCD and a change in symptoms or functional capacity that persists despite GDMT, when selected for rest/stress nuclear MPI, PET is reasonable in preference to SPECT, if available, to improve diagnostic accuracy and decrease the rate of nondiagnostic test results.*29

In patients with CCD and a change in symptoms or functional capacity that persists despite GDMT, exercise treadmill testing can be useful to determine whether the symptoms are consistent with angina pectoris, assess the severity of symptoms, evaluate functional capacity, and guide management.*26,30–32

In patients with CCD undergoing stress PET MPI or stress CMR imaging, the addition of myocardial blood flow reserve (MBFR) can be useful to improve diagnostic accuracy and enhance risk stratification.*18–23

In patients with CCD and a change in symptoms or functional capacity that persists despite GDMT, and who have had previous coronary revascularization, coronary CT angiography (CCTA) is reasonable to evaluate bypass graft or stent patency (for stents ≥3 mm).*33–37

content.title: 3.2. Risk Stratification and Relationship to Treatment Selection
section_headings: 3.2. Risk Stratification and Relationship to Treatment Selection
content.narrative_summary:
In patients with chronic coronary disease (CCD), noninvasive or invasive testing alone is insufficient to accurately risk stratify an individual’s annual risk of cardiovascular death or nonfatal MI. Clinicians should integrate cardiovascular test results with demographic, social, and medical variables (Table 5) and apply validated risk prediction models to estimate annual risk. Although randomized trials have shown that routine revascularization does not reduce major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), a symptom- and integrated risk-based approach may identify patient subsets—such as those with persistent angina, reduced LV function, or heart failure—who may benefit from revascularization.

Noninvasive test results alone are insufficient to risk stratify CCD, and adding clinical variables improves prediction. In an externally validated cohort undergoing exercise stress testing, the Duke Treadmill Score had a c-index of 0.62 for all-cause mortality; adding clinical variables improved discrimination (c-index=0.83) and reclassified 64% of low-risk scores to intermediate/high risk. Externally validated scores lack some functional and anatomic testing modalities, but observational and secondary analyses from randomized trials consistently ...

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Risk Stratification and Relationship to Treatment Selection

rows.recommendation: In patients with CCD, it is recommended that risk stratification incorporate all available information, including noninvasive, invasive, or both cardiovascular diagnostic testing results or use validated risk scores to classify patients as low (<1%), intermediate (1%-3%), or high (>3%) yearly risk for cardiovascular death or nonfatal MI.1-4
In patients with CCD, optimization of GDMT is recommended to reduce MACE.*5-7
In patients with CCD with newly reduced LV systolic function, clinical heart failure, or both, ICA is recommended to assess coronary anatomy and guide potential revascularization.8,9

In patients with CCD, ICA for risk stratification is not routinely recommended in patients without LV systolic dysfunction, heart failure, stable chest pain refractory to GDMT, and/or noninvasive testing suggestive of significant (>50%) left main disease.5-7,10,11

content.title: 4. TREATMENT
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis outlines treatment goals for chronic coronary disease (CCD) to prolong survival and improve quality of life by reducing cardiac death, nonfatal ischemic events, atherosclerosis progression, and symptoms/functional limitations, while considering patient preferences, potential complications, and costs. It emphasizes shared decision-making, global risk assessment (including social determinants of health), symptom and functional evaluation, patient education, and a team-based approach. The supportive text details the heterogeneous CCD patient population, objectives of routine follow-up (monitor new or worsened symptoms, functional status changes, QOL decline, adherence to lifestyle and medical interventions including physical activity, nutrition, weight management, and pharmacotherapy), use of telehealth and algorithmically driven disease-management programs, the role of revascularization and antianginal therapy in symptom reduction, and the application of validated patient-reported health status measures to quantify symptom burden and standardize assessments.

2. In patients with CCD, use of a validated CCD-specific patient-reported health status measure may be reasonable to assess symptoms, functional status, and QOL.

content.title: 4.1.2. Patient Education
content.narrative_summary: Randomized trials and meta-analyses demonstrate that a patient-centered, multidisciplinary, team-based approach improves patient self-efficacy, quality of life, and ASCVD risk factor management versus usual care, facilitating behavior change such as weight loss and tobacco cessation, and may be more cost-effective. Health care resource utilization among patients managed by different provider types is comparable, and telehealth, patient education sessions, specialty clinics, medication therapy management, and decision support tools are effective strategies. Patient education defined as imparting information to change health behaviors improves knowledge and may facilitate lifestyle changes, though effects on mortality and hospitalizations are less clear. Evidence gaps in comparative effectiveness of educational interventions remain.

rows.recommendation: Patients with CCD should receive ongoing individualized education on symptom management, lifestyle changes, and SDOH risk factors to improve knowledge and facilitate behavior change.
Patients with CCD should receive ongoing individualized education on medication adherence to improve knowledge and facilitate behavior change.

content.narrative_summary: This page introduces guideline-directed management and therapy for chronic coronary disease focusing on nutrition and supplements. It presents a structured table of six recommendations on dietary modifications and the (lack of) benefit of nutrition supplements. Below the table, a synopsis summarizes evidence supporting dietary behavior changes to reduce acute cardiovascular events, defines nutritional supplements per the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, and begins recommendation-specific supportive text on Mediterranean-type dietary patterns.

rows.recommendation: In patients with CCD, a diet emphasizing vegetables, fruits, legumes, nuts, whole grains, and lean protein is recommended to reduce the risk of CVD events.*1–4

In patients with CCD, reducing the percentage of calories from saturated fat (<6% of total calories) and replacing with dietary monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fat, complex carbohydrates, and dietary fiber can be beneficial to reduce the risk of CVD events.*1–6

In patients with CCD, minimization of sodium (<2,300 mg/d; optimally 1,500 mg/d) and minimization of processed meats (eg, cured bacon, hot dogs) can be beneficial to reduce the risk of CVD events.*2,3,6,7

In patients with CCD, limiting refined carbohydrates (eg, containing <25% whole grain by weight, including refined cold ready-to-eat breakfast cereal, white bread, white rice), and sugar-sweetened beverages (eg, soft drinks, energy drinks, fruit drinks with added sugars) can be beneficial to reduce the risk of CVD events.*2–4,6,8
In patients with CCD, the intake of trans fat should be avoided because trans fat is associated with increased morbidity and mortality rates.*9,10

In patients with CCD, the use of nonprescription or dietary supplements, including omega-3 fatty acid, vitamins C, D, E, beta-carotene, and calcium, is not beneficial to reduce the risk of acute CVD events.*11–22

content.title: 4.2.3. Tobacco Products
content.narrative_summary: Tobacco smoke exposure, particularly cigarette smoking, is a leading cause of cardiovascular disease and events in persons with chronic coronary disease (CCD). Cigarette smoke adversely affects endothelial function, promotes atherosclerosis, and is prothrombotic. Smoking cessation leads to short-term benefits including decreased heart rate and blood pressure and improved endothelial function, and cohort studies in CCD show reductions in death (36%) and myocardial infarction (32%). Pharmacotherapy and behavioral therapy increase cessation success; smokeless tobacco has mixed results but may carry some CHD risk.

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with CCD, tobacco use should be assessed at every health care visit to facilitate identification of those who may benefit from behavioral or pharmacologic interventions.*1–3
2. Patients with CCD who regularly smoke tobacco should be advised to quit at every visit.*4

3. In patients with CCD who regularly smoke tobacco, behavioral interventions are recommended to maximize cessation rates in combination with pharmacotherapy, including bupropion, varenicline, or combination long- and short-acting nicotine replacement therapy (NRT).*5–7
4. In patients with CCD who regularly smoke tobacco, varenicline may be considered versus bupropion or NRT to increase cessation rates.*6

5. In patients with CCD who regularly smoke tobacco, the short-term use of nicotine-containing e-cigarettes may be considered to aid smoking cessation, although the risk of sustained use and unknown long-term safety may outweigh the benefits.*8–10
6. Patients with CCD should avoid secondhand smoke exposure to reduce risk of cardiovascular events.*11,12

content.narrative_summary: This page presents narrative points 2–4 of a section on smoking cessation: 2. content.title: 4.2.5 Sexual Health and Activity

content.title: Recommendations for Lipid Management
content.narrative_summary: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors should not be used concomitantly with nitrate medications due to the potential for severe hypotension. Sildenafil and vardenafil have half-lives of approximately 4 hours, while tadalafil is long-acting with a half-life of 17.5 hours. Patients on sildenafil or vardenafil should avoid taking nitroglycerin for ≥24 hours (≥48 hours for tadalafil). In patients on long-acting nitrate therapy who wish to use a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor, the decision should be guided by the need for continued nitrate therapy versus alternative options available to the treating clinician. The section then introduces lipid management.

rows.recommendation: In patients with CCD, high-intensity statin therapy is recommended with the aim of achieving a ≥50% reduction in LDL-C levels to reduce the risk of MACE.

In patients in whom high-intensity statin therapy is contraindicated or not tolerated, moderate-intensity statin therapy is recommended with the aim of achieving a 30% to 49% reduction in LDL-C levels to reduce the risk of MACE.

In patients with CCD, adherence to changes in lifestyle and effects of lipid-lowering medication should be assessed by measurement of fasting lipids in 4 to 12 weeks after statin initiation or dose adjustment and then every 3 to 12 months thereafter based on need to assess response or adherence to therapy.
In patients with CCD, the use of generic formulations of maximally tolerated statin therapy is projected to be cost saving.

In patients with CCD who are judged to be at very high risk (Table 10) and on maximally tolerated statin therapy with an LDL-C level ≥70 mg/dL (≥1.8 mmol/L), ezetimibe can be beneficial to further reduce the risk of MACE.
In patients with CCD, addition of generic ezetimibe to maximally tolerated statin therapy in appropriately selected patients is projected to be of high economic value at US prices.

In patients with CCD who are judged to be at very high risk (Table 10) and who have an LDL-C level ≥70 mg/dL (≥1.8 mmol/L), or a non–high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) level ≥100 mg/dL (≥2.6 mmol/L), on maximally tolerated statin and ezetimibe, a PCSK9 monoclonal antibody can be beneficial to further reduce the risk of MACE.
In patients with CCD who are very high risk, the use of PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies is projected to be of uncertain economic value at US prices.

In patients with CCD on maximally tolerated statin therapy with an LDL-C level <100 mg/dL (<2.6 mmol/L) and a persistent fasting triglyceride level of 150 to 499 mg/dL (1.7–5.6 mmol/L) after addressing secondary causes, icosapent ethyl may be considered to further reduce the risk of MACE and cardiovascular death.

In patients with CCD who are not at very high risk and on maximally tolerated statin therapy with an LDL-C level ≥70 mg/dL (≥1.8 mmol/L), it may be reasonable to add ezetimibe to further reduce the risk of MACE.

In patients with CCD on maximally tolerated statin therapy who have an LDL-C level ≥70 mg/dL (≥1.8 mmol/L), and in whom ezetimibe and PCSK9 monoclonal antibody are deemed insufficient or not tolerated, it may be reasonable to add bempedoic acid or inclisiran (in place of PCSK9 monoclonal antibody) to further reduce LDL-C levels.
In patients with CCD receiving statin therapy, adding niacin, or fenofibrate or dietary supplements containing omega-3 fatty acids, are not beneficial in reducing cardiovascular risk.

content.title: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Chronic Coronary Disease Guideline
content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis reviews that LDL-C is a primary driver of atherosclerotic disease and high-intensity statin therapy is preferred to reduce LDL-C ≥50% and lower cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Despite maximal statin therapy, residual risk remains in patients with chronic coronary disease, and adding nonstatins (e.g., ezetimibe, PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies, icosapent ethyl) can further reduce risk. Clinicians should prioritize ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors for additional LDL-C lowering, monitor lipid response, adherence, and persistence. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text provides evidence from the CTT meta-analysis showing a 15% reduction in major vascular events with high- versus moderate-intensity statins, defines statin intolerance and LDL-C lowering goals (≥50%), discusses monitoring frequency, economic value in QALYs, and introduces the IMPROVE-IT trial addition of ezetimibe.

content.narrative_summary: The narrative continues from prior discussion of ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors. An analysis using the TIMI Risk Score for Secondary Prevention (TRS 2°P) showed that adding ezetimibe to statin therapy yielded greater relative and absolute ASCVD risk reduction in patients with ≥3 high-risk features. No RCT directly compared an ezetimibe-first strategy with PCSK9 monoclonal antibody initiation, but clinicians are advised to add ezetimibe before PCSK9 therapy given its generic availability, oral dosing, and proven safety. Generic ezetimibe (<$10/month) can lower LDL-C to <70 mg/dL and is highly cost-effective, though sensitive to assumptions. Very high-risk ASCVD is defined in Table 10. The FOURIER and ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trials demonstrated that evolocumab and alirocumab each reduced cardiovascular events by ≈15%, with greater absolute benefit in very high-risk patients and no increase in neurocognitive adverse effects. Injection site reactions occur, and long-term safety data are limited. Maximal LDL-C–lowering therapy should include maximally tolerated statin plus ezetimibe, with PCSK9 inhibitors added if ≥25% further LDL-C reduction is needed.

content.title: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Chronic Coronary Disease Guideline
content.narrative_summary: Hypertension is a prevalent comorbidity in individuals with chronic coronary disease (CCD), affecting over 60%, and is a well-established risk factor for cardiovascular disease (CVD). Those with CCD and hypertension have higher mortality and morbidity compared with normotensive CCD patients. Treatment with lifestyle modifications and medication helps control hypertension and reduces subsequent risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). These recommendations apply specifically to individuals with CCD and hypertension, with additional guidance on nutritional therapies in Section 4.2.1 and on physical activity and cardiac rehabilitation in Sections 4.2.10–4.2.11. Lifestyle strategies include weight loss, a heart-healthy diet rich in fruits and vegetables, reduced sodium, increased physical activity, and reduced alcohol intake. Lowering systolic blood pressure (BP) to <130 mm Hg reduces CVD complications by approximately 25% and all-cause mortality by 27%, with optimal diastolic BP in the range of 70–80 mm Hg. Clinical trials such as HOPE, INVEST, and EUROPA demonstrate benefits of ACE inhibitors, CCBs, beta blockers, and thiazide diuretics in high-risk and CCD populations.

rows.recommendation: In adults with CCD, nonpharmacologic strategies are recommended as first-line therapy to lower BP in those with elevated BP (120–129/<80 mm Hg) (see Table 12).*1–9
In adults with CCD who have hypertension, a BP target of <130/<80 mm Hg is recommended to reduce CVD events and all-cause death.*10–14

In adults with CCD and hypertension (systolic BP ≥130 and/or diastolic BP ≥80 mm Hg), in addition to nonpharmacological strategies, GDMT angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARB), or beta blockers are recommended as first-line therapy for compelling indications (eg, recent MI or angina), with additional antihypertensive medications (eg, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers [CCB], long-acting thiazide diuretics, and/or mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists) added as needed to optimize BP control.*13,18

content.narrative_summary: The page begins mid-discussion of GDMT antihypertensive therapy in CCD, stating that beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs are recommended first-line, listing specific beta-blockers and noting atenolol may be inferior, with thiazide diuretics, CCBs, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists added if BP remains uncontrolled. After the recommendations table for SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists, the Synopsis summarizes that comprehensive cardiovascular risk reduction strategies in CCD and type 2 diabetes—including SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists—improve glycemic control, promote weight loss, slow kidney disease progression, and reduce cardiovascular events despite persistently high event rates.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Use of SGLT2 Inhibitors and GLP-1 Receptor Agonists

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with CCD who have type 2 diabetes, the use of either an SGLT2 inhibitor1-8 or a GLP-1 receptor agonist9-17 with proven cardiovascular benefit is recommended to reduce the risk of MACE.
2. In patients with CCD and type 2 diabetes, addition of a GLP-1 receptor agonist at US prices is projected to be of high value compared with standard of care.18
3. In patients with CCD and type 2 diabetes, addition of an SGLT2 inhibitor at US prices is projected to be of intermediate value compared with standard of care.18

4. In patients with CCD and heart failure with LVEF ≤40%, use of an SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended to reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization19-22 and to improve QOL,23,24 irrespective of diabetes status.*
5. In patients with CCD and heart failure with LVEF ≤40%, addition of an SGLT2 inhibitor to GDMT, irrespective of diabetes status, is projected to be of intermediate value at US prices.25,26

6. In patients with CCD and heart failure with LVEF >40%, use of an SGLT2 inhibitor can be beneficial in decreasing heart failure hospitalizations27,28 and to improve QOL,4,29 irrespective of diabetes status.
7. In patients with CCD and heart failure with LVEF >40%, addition of an SGLT2 inhibitor to GDMT, irrespective of diabetes status, is projected to be of uncertain value at US prices.30

In patients with CCD and severe obesity who have not met weight loss goals with lifestyle and pharmacologic intervention, and who have acceptable surgical risk, referral for consideration of a bariatric procedure is reasonable for weight loss and cardiovascular risk factor reduction.
In patients with CCD, use of sympathomimetic weight loss drugs is potentially harmful.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of physical activity in chronic coronary disease, noting observational and interventional studies in heart transplant recipients and patients with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) showing benefits of high-intensity interval training and cardiac rehabilitation (CR) on functional capacity, quality of life (QOL), and major adverse cardiovascular events. For patients with CCD who do not have contraindications, lower-intensity lifestyle activities (eg, walking breaks at work) to reduce sedentary behavior (ie, sitting time) are reasonable to improve functional capacity and reduce cardiovascular risk, especially in individuals with low levels of habitual leisure time physical activity.

content.title: 4.2.12. Environmental Exposures
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: Adverse environmental exposures such as air pollution, extremes of ambient temperature, and excess noise should be systematically assessed in patients with chronic coronary disease (CCD). Ecological studies link ambient air pollution (notably PM2.5 from transportation exhaust or wildfire smoke) and extreme temperatures with increased cardiovascular events and mortality. Clinicians should identify at-risk individuals, provide guidance on medication titration (eg, loop diuretics), and encourage controlled-temperature environments during weather extremes. Observational data on noise reduction are limited. Environmental exposures disproportionately affect racial and ethnic minorities and individuals of low socioeconomic status, and policy interventions may mitigate these disparities. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text elaborates on the associations between particulate matter, heat waves, and cardiovascular outcomes.

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with CCD, minimization of exposure to ambient air pollution is reasonable to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events.
2. In patients with CCD, minimization of climate-related exposures (eg, extreme temperatures, wildfire smoke) may be reasonable to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Antiplatelet Therapy and Oral Anticoagulants

rows.recommendation: In patients with CCD and no indication for oral anticoagulant therapy, low-dose aspirin 81 mg (75–100 mg) is recommended to reduce atherosclerotic events.*1–3

In patients with CCD treated with PCI, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) consisting of aspirin and clopidogrel for 6 months post PCI followed by single antiplatelet therapy (SAPT) is indicated to reduce MACE and bleeding events.*4–7

In select patients with CCD treated with PCI and a drug-eluting stent (DES) who have completed a 1- to 3-month course of DAPT, P2Y₁₂ inhibitor monotherapy for at least 12 months is reasonable to reduce bleeding risk.*8–12
In patients with CCD who have had a previous MI and are at low bleeding risk, extended DAPT beyond 12 months for a period of up to 3 years may be reasonable to reduce MACE.*13,14
In patients with CCD and a previous history of MI without a history of stroke, transient ischemic attack (TIA), or ICH, vorapaxar may be added to aspirin therapy to reduce MACE.*15–17
In patients with CCD, the use of DAPT after CABG may be useful to reduce the incidence of saphenous vein graft occlusion.*18
In patients with CCD without recent ACS or a PCI-related indication for DAPT, the addition of clopidogrel to aspirin therapy is not useful to reduce MACE.*19
In patients with CCD and previous stroke, TIA, or ICH, vorapaxar should not be added to DAPT because of increased risk of major bleeding and ICH.*15,20
In patients with CCD and previous stroke, TIA, or ICH, prasugrel should not be used because of risk of significant or fatal bleeding.*21
In patients with CCD, chronic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should not be used because of increased cardiovascular and bleeding complications.*22

In patients with CCD who have undergone elective PCI and who require oral anticoagulant therapy, DAPT for 1 to 4 weeks followed by clopidogrel alone for 6 months should be administered in addition to DOAC.†23

In patients with CCD who have undergone PCI and who require oral anticoagulant therapy, continuing aspirin in addition to clopidogrel for up to 1 month is reasonable if the patient has a high thrombotic risk and low bleeding risk.*23–25

content.title: 4.3.2. Beta Blockers
content.narrative_summary: The prose summarizes beta-blockers’ mechanisms in chronic coronary disease (CCD), including reduced myocardial oxygen demand, improved ischemic threshold, and prevention of maladaptive left ventricular remodeling. It defines the CCD population with or without prior myocardial infarction (MI) or left ventricular systolic dysfunction. The text notes strongest evidence for benefit in patients with LV systolic dysfunction, ongoing trials to clarify duration of therapy in post-MI patients with preserved function, and other indications such as angina, uncontrolled hypertension, and arrhythmias. It recommends comprehensive symptom and comorbidity assessment given beta-blockers’ antianginal, antihypertensive, and chronotropic effects. Key randomized controlled trials (e.g., CIBIS-II, COPERNICUS, MERIT-HF) demonstrated efficacy of bisoprolol, metoprolol succinate, and carvedilol in reducing cardiovascular death and MACE, with dose titrations to target levels.

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with CCD and LVEF ≤40% with or without previous MI, the use of beta-blocker therapy is recommended to reduce the risk of future MACE, including cardiovascular death.
2. In patients with CCD and LVEF <50%, the use of sustained release metoprolol succinate, carvedilol, or bisoprolol with titration to target doses is recommended in preference to other beta blockers.

3. In patients with CCD who were initiated on beta-blocker therapy for previous MI without a history of or current LVEF ≤50%, angina, arrhythmias, or uncontrolled hypertension, it may be reasonable to reassess the indication for long-term (>1 year) use of beta-blocker therapy for reducing MACE.
4. In patients with CCD without previous MI or LVEF ≤50%, the use of beta-blocker therapy is not beneficial in reducing MACE, in the absence of another primary indication for beta-blocker therapy.

content.narrative_summary: The section highlights that respiratory infections such as influenza, pneumococcal pneumonia, and COVID-19 contribute to major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and all-cause death in patients with chronic coronary disease (CCD). Proinflammatory mediators, sympathetic activation, and coagulation cascade activation from these infections may precipitate plaque rupture. Vaccination against these pathogens not only improves clinical outcomes but also reduces hospitalization and health care costs, with randomized clinical trials showing the greatest benefit in high-risk populations including those with advanced age or CCD.

content.title: 5.1. Revascularization
content.narrative_summary: The management of patients with chronic coronary disease (CCD) and stable angina is threefold: relief of symptoms, prevention of nonfatal events such as myocardial infarction, and improving long-term survival. While guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) is often effective, revascularization yields greater improvement in angina and quality of life than medical therapy alone and lowers the risk of cardiovascular death, MI, and urgent revascularization, particularly among patients with multivessel disease. The effect on survival is more nuanced, with benefits most clearly demonstrated in subgroups such as those with severe LV dysfunction or left main disease.

rows.recommendation: In patients with CCD and lifestyle-limiting angina despite GDMT and with significant coronary artery stenoses amenable to revascularization, revascularization is recommended to improve symptoms.

In patients with CCD who have significant left main disease or multivessel disease with severe LV dysfunction (LVEF ≤ 35%), CABG in addition to medical therapy is recommended over medical therapy alone to improve survival.
In patients with CCD and multivessel disease with severe LV dysfunction, CABG added to optimal medical therapy is of intermediate economic value compared with medical therapy alone.

In patients with CCD and multivessel CAD appropriate for either CABG or PCI, revascularization in addition to GDMT is reasonable to lower the risk of cardiovascular events such as spontaneous MI, unplanned urgent revascularizations, or cardiac death.
In selected patients with CCD and significant left main stenosis for whom PCI can provide equivalent revascularization to that possible with CABG, PCI is reasonable to improve survival.

In patients with CCD who have angina or an anginal equivalent, no previous evaluation for ischemia, and angiographically intermediate stenoses, the use of FFR or other proven nonhyperemic pressure ratios (eg, iFR) is recommended before proceeding with PCI.

In patients with CCD undergoing coronary angiography without previous stress testing, the use of invasive FFR to evaluate angiographically intermediate coronary stenoses before proceeding with PCI is a high economic value intervention.

In patients with CCD with complex 3-vessel disease or for whom the optimal treatment strategy is unclear, a Heart Team approach that includes representatives from interventional cardiology and cardiac surgery is recommended to improve patient outcomes.

content.narrative_summary: Continuation of narrative regarding outcomes of revascularization in chronic coronary disease (CCD). Reports that patients randomized to PCI in the ISCHEMIA trial had worse baseline Seattle Angina Questionnaire scores but greater improvements over conservative management; ORBITA showed PCI reduced ischemia but quality-of-life benefits over placebo; pooled FAME and FAME-2 analyses associated lower FFR with magnitudes of QOL improvement. Meta-analyses indicate no overall all-cause mortality benefit of revascularization in contemporary CCD, citing ACME-2, FAME-2, and ISCHEMIA mortality rates. Two subgroups with multivessel disease and left ventricular dysfunction may benefit. The STICH trial demonstrated improved 10-year survival with CABG in ischemic cardiomyopathy, while REVIVED-BCIS2 found no MACE improvement with PCI in severe LV dysfunction. Economic modeling from STICH data showed CABG cost-effectiveness versus medical therapy (≈$63,989 per QALY). Clinical events such as nonfatal MI, unstable angina, and urgent revascularization correlate with ischemia severity; MASS II showed lower 10-year cardiac death rates after CABG or PCI versus medical therapy alone. content.title: 5.2. Revascularization: PCI Versus CABG
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: The section outlines fundamental differences between CABG and PCI in restoring blood flow to ischemic myocardium. CABG provides field protection via bypass grafts that extend beyond diseased native segments and reduces spontaneous MI and repeat revascularization compared with PCI. Certain subgroups (eg, those with complex or diffuse coronary disease and patients with diabetes) derive a survival benefit from CABG over PCI. Revascularization decisions should be guided by Heart Team deliberations (Section 4.1.3) considering available evidence, patient risk profile, and life expectancy. Recommendation‐Specific Supportive Text: 1. The SYNTAX trial showed higher MACE and 5-year mortality with PCI versus CABG in left main and high‐complexity disease (SYNTAX score >33). 2. The 10-year SYNTAX follow‐up confirmed a 40% higher mortality with PCI compared to CABG in triple-vessel disease; pooled RCT data (11,518 patients) demonstrated a mortality benefit with CABG and identified SYNTAX score as a significant modifier of treatment effect.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Revascularization: PCI Versus CABG

rows.recommendation: In patients with CCD who require revascularization for significant left main involvement associated with high-complexity CAD, CABG is recommended in preference to PCI to improve survival.*1,2
In patients with CCD who require revascularization for multivessel CAD with complex and diffuse CAD (eg, SYNTAX score >33), it is reasonable to choose CABG over PCI to improve survival.*1,3-6
In patients with CCD who are appropriate for revascularization but poor candidates for surgery, it is reasonable to choose PCI over CABG to improve symptoms and reduce MACE.7-9

In patients with CCD, diabetes, and multivessel CAD with involvement of the left anterior descending artery who are appropriate candidates for CABG, CABG (with a left internal mammary artery to the left anterior descending artery) is recommended in preference to PCI to reduce mortality and repeat revascularizations.*5,10-17
In patients with CCD and diabetes who have left main stenosis and low- or intermediate-complexity CAD (eg, SYNTAX score ≤33), PCI may be considered as an alternative to CABG to reduce MACE.*10,18

content.title: Synopsis
content.narrative_summary: This page summarizes spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) as an underrecognized cause of myocardial infarction, particularly affecting younger women with few traditional atherosclerotic risk factors. Triggers include pregnancy, intense physical exertion, and emotional stress. Pregnancy‐associated SCAD carries a worse prognosis, and management focuses on conservative therapy, with revascularization reserved for select unstable cases. Dual antiplatelet therapy after stenting should follow standard guidelines, balancing bleeding risk in premenopausal women. Supportive text describes recurrence of SCAD—rates up to 26.9% at one year and 27% at five years—often triggered by exertion or psychosocial stress, and reports a high prevalence of extracoronary vascular abnormalities such as fibromuscular dysplasia and aneurysms, underscoring the role of vascular imaging.

content.narrative_summary: Nonobstructive CAD (INOCA) is present in over 50% of patients undergoing elective coronary angiography and is associated with increased risk of all‐cause death and myocardial infarction. INOCA refers to myocardial ischemia caused by coronary vasomotor dysfunction without obstructive CAD, including microvascular angina (due to microvascular dysfunction) and vasospastic angina (due to dynamic epicardial coronary obstruction). Diagnostic criteria for microvascular angina are outlined by the COVADIS group (Table 15), and criteria for vasospastic angina are in Table 16. For imaging recommendations in nonobstructive CAD, see Section 3.1. Invasive coronary physiology testing is feasible and safe, providing clear diagnostic utility in identifying specific INOCA endotypes.

Definitive diagnosis if all four criteria are met.

content.title: 6.7. Chronic Kidney Disease
content.narrative_summary: CKD increases the risk of CAD progression and is associated with poor outcomes, including a ~20% annual mortality rate in hemodialysis, advanced atherosclerotic plaque features, and less accurate noninvasive testing. Underrepresentation in trials and inconsistent CKD definitions limit data on pharmacological and interventional therapies, but patients should receive similar medical therapy with a team-based approach. In the ISCHEMIA-CKD trial, revascularization did not improve outcomes in patients with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2 or on dialysis. When PCI is performed, efforts should focus on avoiding nephrotoxic agents, ensuring adequate hydration before iodinated contrast, minimizing contrast volume, and using high-dose statins to reduce contrast-induced acute kidney injury.

rows.recommendation: In patients with CCD and CKD, measures should be taken to minimize the risk of treatment-related acute kidney injury.

content.narrative_summary: HIV and other chronic inflammatory conditions accelerate atherosclerosis and premature cardiovascular disease and are recognized as risk-enhancing factors. Patients with HIV have higher rates of coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction compared with age- and sex-matched controls due to HIV itself, antiretroviral therapy, and traditional risk factors. Newer antiretroviral regimens improve lipid profiles and subclinical atherosclerosis markers. Treatments for autoimmune diseases can adversely affect lipids; therefore, steroid-sparing agents should be prioritized and multidisciplinary care including infectious disease and rheumatology expertise is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for HIV and Autoimmune Disorders

rows.recommendation: 1. In adults with CCD and HIV, antiretroviral therapy is beneficial to decrease the risk of cardiovascular events.1,2

2. In adults with CCD and HIV, it is reasonable to choose antiretroviral therapy regimens associated with more favorable lipid and cardiovascular risk profiles with consideration of drug-drug interactions.3-5
3. In adults with CCD and HIV, lovastatin or simvastatin should not be administered with protease inhibitors as this may cause harm.6,7
4. In adults with CCD and rheumatoid arthritis, initiation and maintenance of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs is beneficial to decrease the risk of cardiovascular events.8-11

5. In adults with CCD and autoimmune diseases, treatment with biologics and other immune modulating therapies that reduce disease activity may be considered to decrease the risk of cardiovascular events.10,11
6. In patients with CCD and rheumatoid arthritis, high-dose glucocorticoids should not be used long term if alternative therapies are available because of increased cardiovascular risk.11,12

section_headings: 6.9. Cardiac Allograft Vasculopathy in Heart Transplant Recipients
content.narrative_summary: Post–heart transplant cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is the leading cause of long-term mortality and retransplantation, developing in approximately 30% of patients by 5 years and 50% by 10 years. Coronary angiography, often with intravascular ultrasound, is the standard for diagnosis. Management includes lifestyle modification, optimal control of cardiovascular risk factors, and secondary prevention with statins and aspirin. In patients with severe or proximal lesions, PCI with second-generation DES may reduce restenosis; CABG is infrequently used, and retransplantation is reserved for advanced cases. Early initiation of immunosuppressive agents such as mycophenolate mofetil or calcineurin inhibitors may slow CAV progression but may increase rejection risk.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Cardiac Allograft Vasculopathy in Heart Transplant Recipients

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with cardiac allograft vasculopathy, statins are recommended for secondary prevention to reduce MACE.
2. In patients with cardiac allograft vasculopathy, aspirin can be beneficial for secondary prevention to reduce MACE.

3. In patients with severe cardiac allograft vasculopathy, revascularization is reasonable in those with suitable anatomy to potentially mitigate the adverse long-term consequences of cardiac allograft vasculopathy.

content.title: 7. PATIENT FOLLOW-UP: MONITORING AND MANAGING SYMPTOMS
section_headings: 7.1. Follow-Up Plan and Testing in Stable Patients
content.narrative_summary: This section provides a synopsis emphasizing that patients with chronic coronary disease (CCD) are at elevated risk for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and should be observed periodically in the outpatient setting. Central management includes long-term risk factor modification and optimized guideline‐directed medical therapy (GDMT) with shared decision-making among care teams. Follow-up testing should be reserved for significant changes in symptoms or clinical status, with periodic resting 12-lead ECGs providing a baseline for comparison. Recommendation-specific supportive text details several randomized trials of telehealth and lifestyle‐intervention programs (Hartcoach, Proactive Heart, MoodCare) showing modest improvements in physical and psychological outcomes, and begins description of the RESPONCE-2 trial of ruxolitinib in polycythemia vera, cutting off mid-sentence.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Follow-Up Plan and Testing in Stable Patients

rows.recommendation: In stable patients with CCD and with previous ACS or coronary revascularization, referral to telehealth programs, community-based programs, or both for lifestyle interventions may be reasonable as an adjunct to usual care to improve management of cardiovascular risk factors.1-7

In patients with CCD without a change in clinical or functional status on optimized GDMT, routine periodic testing with coronary CTA or stress testing with or without imaging is not recommended to guide therapeutic decision-making.8-10
In patients with CCD without a change in clinical or functional status, routine periodic reassessment of LV function is not recommended to guide therapeutic decision-making.11,12
In patients with CCD without a change in clinical or functional status, routine periodic invasive coronary angiography should not be performed to guide therapeutic decision-making.13-17
